intro: Istanbul lies on both banks of the Bosphorus, the strait between the Black Sea and the Sea of Marmara, half in Europe and half in Asia. For sixteen centuries it was a capital, of the Roman and Byzantine emperors as Constantinople and of the Ottoman sultans after them. Its old peninsula, between the Golden Horn and the sea, holds the Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque, Topkapı Palace and the Grand Bazaar. Today it is the largest city of Turkey, with more than fifteen million people.

overview: The old city of Istanbul is a peninsula shaped like a horn, with the Golden Horn to the north, the Sea of Marmara to the south and the Bosphorus at its tip. On its point lies Topkapı Palace above Gülhane Park, and just inland the Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque face each other across Sultanahmet Square, with the long Hippodrome beside them. From there the Divan Yolu, the old imperial road, runs west past the Column of Constantine to the Grand Bazaar, while the streets to the north fall steeply down to Sirkeci, Eminönü, the New Mosque and the Spice Bazaar on the shore of the Golden Horn, where the Galata Bridge crosses to Karaköy.

Instant Istanbul takes you through the heart of it: from the Hagia Sophia along the Divan Yolu to the Column of Constantine and the gate of the Grand Bazaar, down the Ankara Caddesi to Sirkeci, and back along the tram past Gülhane Park and down the lane of wooden houses to the gate of Topkapı Palace. The real streets climb and fall over the hills; in the game the city is flat.
setting: Istanbul spreads along the Bosphorus, the 30-kilometre strait that joins the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara and divides Europe from Asia. On the European side the Golden Horn, a long inlet, cuts the old city off from Galata and Beyoğlu to the north. Three bridges and two tunnels cross the Bosphorus, and the ferries cross it all day.
The climate lies between that of the Mediterranean and the Black Sea: hot, humid summers, cool and wet winters with now and then snow, and winds that blow down the Bosphorus from the north.

history.title: Byzantium
text: Greek settlers from Megara founded Byzantium in the 7th century BC on the point of the peninsula, where Topkapı Palace stands today. From there it guarded the passage between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, and it grew rich on the trade and the fish of the strait.
The Romans took it in, and in 196 the emperor Septimius Severus rebuilt it after a siege, with the Hippodrome.

history.title: Constantinople
text: In 330 Constantine the Great made the city the new capital of the Roman Empire and named it after himself. Justinian rebuilt the Hagia Sophia after the Nika riots of 532, and for a thousand years Constantinople was the largest and richest city of Christendom, behind its land walls.
In 1204 the knights of the Fourth Crusade sacked it, and the Byzantine Empire never fully recovered.

history.title: The Ottoman capital
text: On 29 May 1453 the young Sultan Mehmed II took the city after a siege of 53 days. He made it his capital, turned the Hagia Sophia into a mosque, built Topkapı Palace and the first halls of the Grand Bazaar, and brought people from all over his empire to live there.

Under Süleyman the Magnificent and his architect Mimar Sinan the city filled with mosques, baths and schools, and in the 17th century the Blue Mosque and the New Mosque were added to its skyline. In the 19th century the sultans moved to new palaces along the Bosphorus, and the railway from Europe reached Sirkeci.

history.title: The republic
text: After the First World War the Ottoman Empire fell. In 1923 the Republic of Turkey was proclaimed and Ankara became its capital, and in 1930 the city’s name became Istanbul for everyone.

Since the 1950s it has grown from about a million people to more than fifteen million, spreading far along both shores. Bridges over the Bosphorus came in 1973, 1988 and 2016, and a railway tunnel under it, the Marmaray, in 2013.

today: Istanbul is the largest city of Turkey and its centre of business, culture and trade, home to more than fifteen million people. The old peninsula is the heart of its sights, a World Heritage Site since 1985, while most people live and work in the new districts on both shores.

Visitors come for the Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque, the Basilica Cistern, Topkapı Palace and the bazaars, and for the ferries, the fish sandwiches by the Galata Bridge and the views over the Bosphorus. The T1 tram runs along the Divan Yolu from the Grand Bazaar to Sultanahmet and down to Eminönü.
